overview: “Islamic and Hindu states” is a changing atlas umbrella across parts of South Asia, not one empire or a complete description of its communities. The 1530 and 1600 main outlines include Ahmedabad, Gaur and much of central India; a small coastal patch also appears in 1530. The 1650 outline contracts to east-central India, including Jabalpur, Ramnagar, Nagpur, Raipur and Bastar. These snapshots can preserve outdated political boundaries. Named sultanates, Gond kingdoms, the Mughal Empire and other regional states retain their own histories. Religion alone did not determine a person’s language, occupation or political allegiance.

periods.title: Independent courts and imperial expansion
periods.summary: Gujarat’s sultanate was annexed by Akbar in 1573, before the next atlas snapshot.

periods.title: A repeated outline
periods.summary: The main map shape repeats despite earlier changes in Bengal and Gujarat. Its edges are not a reliable list of independent states.

periods.title: Central Indian courts and buildings
periods.summary: Ramnagar’s seventeenth-century royal buildings show an active Gond court within the later outline.

items.text: At the western end of the early outline, Gujarat’s sultanate came under Mughal rule in 1573. Ahmedabad’s inclusion in the 1600 umbrella should therefore not be read as proof that the same independent sultanate survived. A map snapshot can lag behind a major political change.

Bengal followed a different sequence. The Husain Shahi dynasty fell in 1538, followed by Afghan rulers and Mughal intervention. In 1576 Mughal forces defeated Daud Karrani at Rajmahal. That battle changed the ruling order, but regional resistance and the work of establishing control did not simply disappear in one afternoon.

Central Indian Gond kingdoms developed their own systems of authority. Garha-Katanga was organized through clan-controlled garhs and smaller village groupings. Trapping and exporting elephants brought wealth: a powerful animal could be a diplomatic asset as well as expensive cargo. Several Gond states coexisted; they were not one interchangeable kingdom.

Royal family life could become government. After Dalpat Shah’s death, Durgavati governed Garha-Katanga for her young son, assisted by ministers. She resisted a Mughal invasion and died in 1564. Remembering her only as somebody’s wife or mother misses her own political and military authority.

Food moved with families. The seventeenth-century traveler Peter Mundy described Banjara caravans carrying wheat and rice, in which wives and children traveled alongside traders and their oxen. They bought grain where it cost less and sold it elsewhere. His account gives a glimpse of mobile households that helped connect settled towns and armies to supplies.

Near Garha, a chain of tanks used the slope of the land: overflow from Maharaj Tal fed lower tanks, eventually draining toward the river system. Geologist K.G.Vyas describes five linked tanks that still survive. The landscape did part of the carrying, with gravity supplying the muscle. Individual construction dates are not established for every tank.

Step-wells in the Jabalpur area made water reachable by stairs. Vyas describes stone lining in upper soil layers while sound water-bearing rock below could remain unlined, allowing groundwater to enter. He interprets some nearby tanks without canals as serving drinking and household needs. This is evidence about collecting water, not proof of universal piped supplies or toilets.

At Ramnagar’s Moti Mahal, the royal kitchen, bedrooms, halls and stables belonged to a carefully arranged palace complex. A stepped water feature occupied the central courtyard. Its drainage directed stormwater toward the Narmada. Keeping rain moving away from rooms was an architectural achievement; the surviving description does not establish a citywide sewage system.

The residence of the king’s minister at Ramnagar offered practical comfort as well as status. A high entrance wall screened the interior and blocked strong sunlight. Rooms were arranged around a courtyard, with lower roofs along its inner edge. Privacy and shade mattered in designing a home, even when the resident was an important official.

A sixteenth-century bridal casket associated with Gujarat and Goa or Lisbon combines teak, silver and shimmering mother-of-pearl. Its decorative technique is Indian, while its form follows European models. Objects like this served Portuguese clients, especially in Asia. It is a record of skilled cross-cultural production, not a model of every local wedding gift.

An early seventeenth-century Gujarat pen box carries Persian verses about calligraphy. Shell pieces and a lacquer-like substance decorate a container for writing tools. Such objects were made for local use and export. Learning to form beautiful letters could be celebrated on the very box that held the tools, although an expensive example tells us about patrons rather than universal literacy.

Ramnagar’s 1667 Sanskrit inscription praises Queen Sundari Devi for gardens, ponds and donations and commemorates her temple. Its words present an ideal of generous rulership; they are royal praise, not an independent survey of everyone’s welfare. Archaeologists can compare that written claim with the surviving buildings rather than treating either source as the whole story.

A short phrase from that inscription reads “abhavatsundarī devī rānī tasya mahīpateḥ,” translated “That king had a beautiful queen, Sundari Devi.” This is the published scholarly transliteration of Sanskrit originally carved in Devanagari at Ramnagar in 1667. The modern letters shown here reproduce an edited reading of damaged stone, not its original appearance or everyday Gondi speech.

The inscription also makes skilled people visible. It names the scholar Jayagovinda and associates his family with learned debate and poetic meter; it names Simhasahi, Dayarama and Bhagiratha as the temple’s expert builders. A royal monument required more than a ruler with an idea: scholars and craftspeople supplied specialized knowledge.

ending.text: The 1700 cutoff ends this atlas category, not all its communities or states. Gond royal building at Ramnagar belongs to a continuing regional history. The broad religious label gives way to more specific political stories; families, languages and practical skills outlast changes in map colors.
